target: AG1’s claim that renewables can replace fossil fuels because some countries already get very high shares of electricity from renewables
objection: High renewable shares in small or hydropower-rich countries do not show that large countries can achieve the same replacement level; in large countries like the United States, alternative energy use has historically never exceeded about 20%, so renewables have not yet demonstrated replacement-level performance there.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear energy makes fossil-fuel replacement faster and more feasible because it is low-carbon and land-efficient
objection: Nuclear should not be treated as a reliable solution because accidents such as Fukushima show it is not reliably carbon-free in practice; a major accident can erase the carbon-free gain and cause major harms, undermining the idea that nuclear is a safe feasibility booster.

target: AG2’s claim that a Fukushima-like accident means nuclear power’s carbon-free benefit is not reliable enough to matter
objection: The objection overstates the effect of rare accidents: nuclear’s lifecycle emissions are still far below fossil fuels, and occasional major accidents do not usually cancel the overall long-run low-carbon advantage of nuclear generation.

target: AG2’s inference from low historical renewable shares in large countries to the conclusion that alternatives cannot replace fossil fuels
objection: Low historical adoption levels mostly reflect past constraints such as infrastructure buildout, regulation, investment, and grid integration timelines, not a fundamental inability of alternative energy technologies to reach replacement-level shares when scaled.

target: AG1’s conclusion that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels in general
objection: Fossil fuels are used for much more than electricity—especially transportation, industrial heat, and feedstocks—so decarbonizing electricity alone does not fully replace fossil fuels overall.

target: AG1’s assumption that high shares of renewable/nuclear electricity imply full fossil-fuel replacement
objection: Renewables and nuclear mainly produce electricity, not direct substitutes for transportation fuels or industrial process heat at existing scales, so without major sector conversion fossil fuels are still needed.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energy can broadly displace fossil-fuel use across sectors
objection: Treating power-sector substitution as proof of general fossil-fuel replacement overgeneralizes what renewables and nuclear can actually displace, because they cannot be assumed to replace all fossil uses without extensive sector-specific conversion.

target: AG1’s claim that fossil fuels are not necessary once sectors are converted
objection: A realistic net-zero pathway must cover all sectors over time, and existing fossil-fuel infrastructure—especially natural gas—can provide faster emissions reductions while clean conversion scales, so fossil fuels remain necessary as a bridge.

target: AG2’s claim that replacing non-electric fossil-fuel uses via electrification or synthetic fuels would require too much alternative energy because of conversion losses
objection: In many end uses, especially electric motors and heat pumps, electric technologies deliver the same service with higher efficiency than combustion, so conversion losses do not necessarily mean substantially more alternative energy is needed.

target: AG2’s claim that fossil fuels remain necessary because conversion-based replacement is too demanding
objection: If alternative energy can supply low-carbon transport, heat, and feedstocks through electrification and renewable-derived fuels, then continued fossil-fuel use is not required once those sector conversions occur.

target: AG2’s argument that nuclear is too unsafe to help with transition feasibility
objection: Nuclear is low-carbon and land-efficient, and it can provide firm electricity that supports large-scale electrification and renewable electrofuel production, so it can still improve the feasibility of replacing fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s efficiency argument that electrification offsets conversion losses enough to avoid needing much more energy
objection: Electrification and electrofuel pathways still require low-carbon energy at the time and scale needed for reliability, including firm power, ramping, and backup; average end-use efficiency does not remove those system-level requirements.

target: AG1’s claim that hard-to-electrify sectors can be covered by alternative energy without making fossil fuels necessary
objection: Some major fossil-fuel uses cannot be replaced by electrification alone and require renewable-derived fuels or chemicals, which add extra conversion steps and make full replacement more demanding than the efficiency argument suggests.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that alternatives can make fossil fuels unnecessary as an enduring bridge
objection: Because efficiency does not remove reliability constraints and hard-to-electrify sectors need extra conversion, alternatives cannot be assumed to eliminate the need for fossil fuels during the transition; natural gas can instead serve as a rapid dispatchable bridge using existing infrastructure.

target: AG1’s claim that higher end-use efficiency offsets conversion losses sufficiently
objection: Efficiency gains can be partly cancelled by rebound effects, where lower effective energy costs lead people and firms to use more energy or services, so total low-carbon energy demand may remain large.

target: AG1’s implication that efficiency improvements make fossil fuels unnecessary while alternatives scale
objection: Even if some devices become more efficient, replacement-level alternative energy would still need to supply a dominant share of total energy/services at scale, and if deployment remains below that level, fossil fuels are still needed to fill the gap; natural gas is the practical bridge.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can reliably provide firm low-carbon electricity for large-scale electrification and electrofuel production
objection: Nuclear cannot be safely assumed to provide reliable firm low-carbon electricity at scale because real-world accidents such as Fukushima show it is not reliably carbon-free in practice and can impose major harms.

target: AG1’s conclusion that reliable firm low-carbon electricity can cover transition-era demand without fossil backstops
objection: If nuclear is not reliably firm and carbon-free, then low-carbon electricity alone cannot be counted on to cover ramping and backup needs during the transition, so some fossil backstop is still required.

target: AG1’s overall claim that alternative energies can fully replace fossil fuels on realistic timelines
objection: Effective replacement requires continuous, on-demand energy service; variable renewables alone cannot guarantee that, and if nuclear cannot be relied on for firm capacity, fossil fuels remain necessary as a practical backup during scaling.

target: AG1’s implication that fossil-fuel backup is unnecessary once alternatives are deployed
objection: Because alternatives cannot reliably supply continuous dispatchable capacity on their own, fossil fuels—especially natural gas—remain the appropriate bridge fuel until low-carbon capacity and balancing are fully built out.
